title: Bibliology
summary: These passages show Scripture being taught, treasured, interpreted, and used to form a community. Deuteronomy 6 tells Israel to keep God’s commands in the heart and pass them on in daily life. Psalm 19 praises the Lord’s instruction as a guide, while Psalm 119 describes remembering and living by that instruction. In Luke 24, the risen Jesus interprets Moses and the Prophets in relation to what has happened to him. Second Timothy 3 says the sacred writings instruct and equip; Hebrews 1 speaks of God’s speech through the prophets and in the Son. The passages concern related but distinct things—commands, poetic reflection, scriptural interpretation, and divine speech—and do not by themselves answer later questions about the Bible’s formation or authority.
historical_context: The references span Israel’s instruction and poetry as well as early Christian texts. Deuteronomy 6 commands Israel to remember and teach God’s words in ordinary settings. Psalm 19 and Psalm 119 reflect poetically on the guidance and value of divine instruction. Luke 24 presents Jesus explaining Moses and the Prophets after the resurrection. Second Timothy 3 refers to sacred writings known to Timothy and describes their use in teaching and formation. Hebrews 1 opens by contrasting God’s speech through the prophets with God’s speech in the Son. These passages show how Scripture functions in their own arguments; they do not provide a history of biblical book composition or collection.
canonical_context: Deuteronomy’s commands to remember and teach God’s words are echoed by the Psalms’ praise and meditation on instruction. Luke 24 depicts Jesus interpreting Moses and the Prophets in relation to his story. Second Timothy describes the sacred writings as useful for teaching and equipping, while Hebrews 1 presents the Son within the story of God’s speech through the prophets. The passages connect Israel’s Scriptures with later Christian interpretation and practice, while preserving the differences among law, poetry, Gospel narrative, and theological argument.
literary_context: The theme appears in covenant instruction in Deuteronomy 6, praise and meditation in Psalms 19 and 119, a post-resurrection interpretation scene in Luke 24, pastoral instruction in Second Timothy 3, and the opening argument of Hebrews. Deuteronomy emphasizes teaching and memory; the Psalms voice delight and reflection; Luke narrates interpretation; Second Timothy discusses formation; Hebrews sets prophetic speech beside speech in the Son. These forms shape what each passage contributes to bibliology.
covenantal_significance: Deuteronomy 6 places remembering and teaching God’s commands within Israel’s daily life. The Psalms portray instruction as a source of guidance and a subject for sustained meditation. Luke 24 offers a Christian reading of Moses and the Prophets in relation to Jesus; Second Timothy 3 describes the sacred writings as equipping readers; Hebrews 1 links God’s speech through prophets with God’s speech in the Son. Together the passages connect received Scripture with worship, teaching, interpretation, and practice. They address those themes without establishing a complete doctrine of canon, transmission, or inerrancy.
canonical_role: Bibliology serves as a theological anchor, connecting doctrinal concepts, canonical development, and related passages across Scripture.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Bibliology in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
